title: Part 2, Chapter 13
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Knight of the Grove continues, along with the sensible, original, and peaceful conversation that passed between the two squires

The knights and the squires split into two groups, the squires telling the story of their lives, the knights the story of their loves; but the history reports the servants' conversation first and takes up the masters' afterward. It says that, drawing a little apart from the others, the squire of the Grove said to Sancho, “It’s a hard life we lead and live, señor, we who are squires to knights-errant; truly we eat our bread in the sweat of our faces, which is one of the curses God laid on our first parents.”

“You could also say,” Sancho added, “that we eat it in the chill of our bodies, for who suffers more heat and cold than the wretched squires of knight-errantry? Even that wouldn’t be so bad if we had something to eat, since troubles weigh less when there’s bread; but sometimes we go a day or two without breaking our fast, except on the wind that blows.”

“All of that,” said the squire of the Grove, “can be endured and put up with as long as we have hope of a reward; for unless the knight-errant a man serves is exceptionally unlucky, within a few campaigns the squire will at least find himself paid with a fine governorship of some island or some handsome county.”
“I,” said Sancho, “have already told my master that I’ll be satisfied with the governorship of some island, and he is so noble and so generous that he has promised it to me any number of times.”
“I,” said the squire of the Grove, “will be content with a canonry for my services, and my master has already set one aside for me.”

“Then your master,” said Sancho, “must be a knight in the Church line, able to grant favors of that kind to his good squire; mine is only a layman—though I remember that some clever people, schemers in my opinion, tried to persuade him to work at becoming an archbishop. He, however, would settle for nothing less than emperor; and all the while I was trembling for fear he might take a notion to enter the Church, since I don’t consider myself fit to hold any office in it; for I can tell you, though I look like a man, I’m no better than a beast where the Church is concerned.”

“Well, you’re mistaken there,” said the squire of the Grove, “because those island governorships are not all they’re made out to be. Some are troublesome, some are poor, some are dreary, and even the highest and choicest of them carries a heavy load of cares and worries that lands on the shoulders of the unlucky man whose lot it becomes. Far better it would be for those of us who have taken up this cursed service to go back to our own houses and occupy ourselves there with pleasanter pursuits—hunting, say, or fishing; for what squire in the world is so poor that he doesn’t have a nag, a couple of greyhounds, and a fishing rod to amuse himself with in his own village?”

“I’m not short of any of those things,” said Sancho. “True, I have no nag, but I have an ass worth twice my master’s horse. God send me a bad Easter, and let it be the very next one I see, if I would trade him, even with four bushels of barley thrown into the bargain. You’ll laugh at the value I put on my Dapple—for dapple is the color of my beast. As for greyhounds, I’ll never lack them, for there are plenty and to spare in my town; and besides, sport is all the sweeter when it comes at other people’s expense.”

“Truly and honestly, sir squire,” said the squire of the Grove, “I have made up my mind and resolved to be done with the drunken antics of these knights, go back to my village, and raise my children; for I have three, like three Oriental pearls.”
“I have two,” said Sancho, “fit to be presented to the Pope himself, especially a girl I’m bringing up to be a countess, please God, though over her mother’s objections.”
“And how old is this lady who is being raised to be a countess?” asked the squire of the Grove.
“Fifteen, give or take a couple of years,” answered Sancho; “but she’s as tall as a lance, as fresh as an April morning, and as strong as a porter.”
“Those are qualities fit not only for a countess but for a nymph of the greenwood,” said the squire of the Grove. “Ah, the whoreson strumpet! What strength the rogue must have in her!”

To which Sancho answered, a little sourly, “She’s no strumpet, and neither was her mother, and neither of them ever will be, please God, as long as I live. Speak more politely; for a man brought up among knights-errant, who are courtesy itself, those words of yours don’t strike me as very becoming.”

“Oh, how little you understand about compliments, sir squire,” replied the squire of the Grove. “What! Don’t you know that when a horseman plants a fine lance thrust in the bull down in the plaza, or when anyone does anything especially well, people commonly cry, ‘Ha, the whoreson rascal, how well he did it!’—and that what sounds like an insult in the phrase is in fact high praise? Disown any sons and daughters, señor, who don’t do things that earn their parents compliments of that kind.”

“Then I do disown them,” replied Sancho, “and by that same reasoning you could call me, my children, and my wife all the strumpets in the world, because everything they do and say is of a kind that deserves such praise in the highest degree. And so that I may see them again, I pray God to keep me from mortal sin—or what amounts to the same thing, to deliver me from this dangerous trade of squire that I’ve fallen into a second time, lured and led astray by a purse with a hundred ducats in it that I found one day in the heart of the Sierra Morena; and the devil keeps dangling a bag full of doubloons before my eyes, here, there, everywhere, until at every step I imagine I’m laying my hand on it, hugging it, carrying it home, making investments, drawing interest, and living like a prince; and as long as I’m thinking of that, I make light of all the hardships I put up with from this simpleton of a master of mine, who I know very well is more madman than knight.”

“That’s why they say that ‘greed bursts the bag,’” said the squire of the Grove; “but if you want to talk of madmen, there’s no greater one in the world than my master, for he’s one of those they mean when they say, ‘other men’s troubles kill the ass’: so that another knight may recover the wits he has lost, he turns madman himself and goes hunting for something that, once found, may for all I know blow up in his own face.” “And is he in love, by any chance?” asked Sancho.

“He is,” said the squire of the Grove, “with one Casildea de Vandalia, the rawest and best-roasted lady the whole world could produce; but that rawness isn’t the only foot he limps on, for he has bigger schemes rumbling in his belly, as will come out before many hours have passed.”

“There’s no road so smooth that it doesn’t have a pothole or a snag in it,” said Sancho. “In other houses they cook beans; in mine, whole potfuls. Madness will always have more followers and hangers-on than good sense; but if there’s any truth in the old saying that companions in trouble bring some relief, then I can take comfort from you, since you serve a master as crazy as my own.”
“Crazy but brave,” replied the squire of the Grove, “and more of a rogue than either crazy or brave.”

“Mine isn’t like that,” said Sancho. “I mean, there’s nothing of the rogue in him; on the contrary, he has the soul of a pitcher. He couldn’t think of doing harm to anyone, only good to everybody, and there’s no malice in him at all; a child could convince him it’s night at high noon. And for that simplicity I love him like the core of my own heart, and I can’t bring myself to leave him, no matter what foolish things he does.”

“All the same, brother and señor,” said the squire of the Grove, “when the blind lead the blind, both are in danger of falling into the pit. We’d do better to beat a quiet retreat and get back to our own quarters, for the people who go looking for adventures don’t always find good ones.”

Sancho kept spitting from time to time, and his spittle looked rather sticky and dry. Noticing this, the kindhearted squire of the Grove said, “It seems to me that all this talking of ours is gluing our tongues to the roofs of our mouths; but I have a pretty good loosener hanging from my horse’s saddle-bow.” Getting up, he came back a minute later with a large bota of wine and a meat pie half a yard across—and that is no exaggeration, for it was made from a house rabbit so big that Sancho, feeling its weight, took it for a goat, never mind a kid; and looking at it he said, “And you carry this around with you, señor?”
“Why, what did you expect?” said the other. “Do you take me for some bread-and-water squire? I carry a better larder on my horse’s croup than a general takes with him when he goes on campaign.”

Sancho ate without needing to be coaxed, and in the dark he gulped down mouthfuls as big as the knots on a tether, and said, “You are a true and trusty squire, one of the right sort, lavish and grand, as this banquet shows—which, if it didn’t arrive here by magic, certainly has the look of it; not like me, poor wretch, who carry nothing in my alforjas but a scrap of cheese so hard you could brain a giant with it, and, to keep it company, a few dozen carob pods and about as many hazelnuts and walnuts—all thanks to the austerity of my master and the notion he holds and the rule he follows, that knights-errant must not live or feed themselves on anything but dried fruit and the herbs of the field.”

“On my faith, brother,” said the squire of the Grove, “my stomach was not built for thistles, or wild pears, or forest roots. Let our masters do as they please, with their chivalric notions and laws, and eat what those prescribe; I carry my food basket and this bota hanging from the saddle-bow, whatever they may say; and I worship it so, and love it so dearly, that hardly a moment goes by when I’m not kissing it and hugging it over and over again.” So saying, he put it into Sancho’s hands, who tipped it up, set it to his mouth, and studied the stars for a quarter of an hour; and when he had finished drinking he let his head loll to one side, heaved a deep sigh, and exclaimed, “Ah, the whoreson rogue, how catholic it is!”
“You see there,” said the squire of the Grove on hearing Sancho’s exclamation, “how you’ve just called this wine whoreson by way of praise.”
“Well,” said Sancho, “I admit it, and I grant it’s no insult to call anyone a whoreson when it’s meant as praise. But tell me, señor, by whatever you love best—is this Ciudad Real wine?”
“What a rare wine-taster!” said the squire of the Grove. “From nowhere else, in fact, and it has a few years’ age on it too.”

“Trust me for that,” said Sancho. “Never fear—one way or another I’ll hit on the place it came from. What would you say, sir squire, if I told you I have such a great natural instinct for judging wines that you need only let me smell one and I can tell you for certain its country, its kind, its flavor and soundness, the changes it will go through, and everything else that belongs to a wine? And it’s no wonder, for on my father’s side I’ve had in my family the two finest wine-tasters La Mancha has known in many a long year, and to prove it I’ll tell you something that happened to them. The two of them were given some wine from a cask to try, and were asked their opinion of its condition and quality, whether it was good or bad. One tested it with the tip of his tongue; the other did no more than hold it to his nose. The first said the wine had a flavor of iron; the second said it tasted even more strongly of cordovan leather. The owner insisted the cask was clean and that nothing had been added to the wine that could give it a taste of either iron or leather. Even so, the two great wine-tasters stood by what they had said. Time went on, the wine was sold, and when they came to clean out the cask, they found inside it a little key hanging from a strap of cordovan. So judge for yourself whether a man who comes of that stock has a right to give his opinion in cases like these.”

“And that is exactly why I say,” said the squire of the Grove, “that we should give up chasing adventures; since we have loaves, let’s not go looking for cakes, and let’s get back to our own cribs, for God will find us there if it’s his will.”
“I’ll stay in my master’s service until he reaches Saragossa,” said Sancho; “after that, we’ll see.”

The upshot was that the two squires talked so much and drank so much that sleep had to tie their tongues and temper their thirst, for quenching it was impossible; and so the pair of them dropped off to sleep, still clinging to the nearly empty bota and with half-chewed mouthfuls in their mouths. And there we will leave them for the present, in order to relate what passed between the Knight of the Grove and the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
